name: government_set1_p1
label: Government: set 1 (political concepts and the organs of government)

papers.title: Meaning and Nature of Government: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on meaning and nature of government, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Government as an institution refers to
questions.explanation:
As an institution, government means the legislature, executive and judiciary that make, enforce and interpret laws.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the academic study of the state, its organs and how power is used: That is government as an academic subject.
- the activity or process of ruling a society and making decisions for it: That is government as a process or art.
- the citizens who vote in elections to choose their representatives: Voters are the electorate, not the institutions of government.

options.label: A
options.content: the organs that make, carry out and interpret the laws of a state

options.label: B
options.content: the academic study of the state, its organs and how power is used

options.label: C
options.content: the activity or process of ruling a society and making decisions for it

options.label: D
options.content: the citizens who vote in elections to choose their representatives

questions.stem: Power that is accepted as rightful by the people over whom it is exercised is called
questions.explanation:
Authority is legitimate power: the right to command that people accept.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- force: Force is the use of physical coercion, not accepted right.
- influence: Influence is the ability to persuade without the right to command.
- sovereignty: Sovereignty is the supreme power of the state, not acceptance by the governed.

questions.stem: The process by which people acquire political values and attitudes is known as
questions.explanation:
Political socialisation passes on political values through family, school, media, religion and peers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- political participation: Participation is taking part in political activity, not learning values.
- political culture: Political culture is the set of values itself, not the process of acquiring them.
- political recruitment: Recruitment is the selection of people for political office.

questions.stem: A government is said to be legitimate when
questions.explanation:
Legitimacy is the acceptance by the governed that those in power have the right to rule, often through free elections.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it has a large army: Military strength gives force, not legitimacy.
- it collects taxes regularly: Tax collection does not prove that the people accept the government.
- it has ruled for a long time: Long rule can be maintained by force without acceptance.

options.label: C
options.content: it has ruled for a long time

options.label: D
options.content: the people accept its right to rule

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of government?
questions.explanation:
Functions of government include maintaining law and order, defending the state and providing social services.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Forming political parties: Parties are formed by citizens, not by the government as a function.
- Writing newspaper editorials: Editorials are written by the press.
- Choosing members of pressure groups: Pressure groups recruit their own members.

papers.title: State and Sovereignty: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on state and sovereignty, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an essential feature of a state?
questions.explanation:
A state needs population, territory, government and sovereignty; many states contain several ethnic groups.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A defined territory: Territory is an essential feature of a state.
- A population: Population is an essential feature of a state.
- Sovereignty: Sovereignty is an essential feature of a state.

questions.stem: Sovereignty means
questions.explanation:
Sovereignty is the supreme and final legal authority of the state, internally and externally.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the right of all adult citizens to vote freely in periodic elections: That is the franchise.
- the power of the courts to interpret the laws and settle disputes: That is judicial power, only part of state authority.
- a group of people who share a common culture, language and history: That describes a nation.

options.label: A
options.content: the right of all adult citizens to vote freely in periodic elections

options.label: B
options.content: the power of the courts to interpret the laws and settle disputes

options.label: C
options.content: supreme power of a state over its people and territory, free from external control

options.label: D
options.content: a group of people who share a common culture, language and history

questions.stem: The main difference between a state and a nation is that a state
questions.explanation:
A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state is a sovereign political unit with a government.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- must have a common language: A common language is more typical of a nation.
- must be made up of one ethnic group: States often contain many ethnic groups.
- cannot have a defined territory: A state must have a defined territory.

options.label: B
options.content: must be made up of one ethnic group

options.label: D
options.content: must have sovereignty and a government

questions.stem: Membership of international organisations such as the UN and ECOWAS is a
questions.explanation:
Treaties and international obligations limit what a state can do, restricting its external sovereignty.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- source of the sovereignty of a state: Sovereignty does not come from membership of organisations.
- feature of a nation: It has nothing to do with being a nation.
- form of de facto sovereignty: De facto sovereignty is about who actually holds power within a state.

options.label: A
options.content: limitation on the sovereignty of a state

options.label: B
options.content: source of the sovereignty of a state

questions.stem: A military junta that controls a country after a coup but is not recognised by law exercises
questions.explanation:
De facto sovereignty is power held in fact, whether or not it is legal.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- de jure sovereignty: De jure sovereignty is legal sovereignty, which the junta lacks.
- popular sovereignty: Popular sovereignty rests with the people.
- titular sovereignty: Titular sovereignty is held by a ceremonial head of state.

papers.title: Forms of Government: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on forms of government, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a unitary state, governmental power is
questions.explanation:
In a unitary state the central government is supreme; local bodies get only the powers it delegates.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- shared equally by the centre and the regions under the constitution: That describes federalism.
- held by sovereign member states: That describes a confederation.
- held only by local councils: Local councils exercise only powers delegated by the centre.

options.label: A
options.content: shared equally by the centre and the regions under the constitution

questions.stem: Which country is an example of a federal state in West Africa?
questions.explanation:
Nigeria has a federal constitution with 36 states and a federal government.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone is a unitary state.
- Ghana: Ghana is a unitary state.
- Liberia: Liberia is a unitary state.

questions.stem: In a federation, matters on which both the federal and state governments may legislate are on the
questions.explanation:
The concurrent list contains shared subjects; federal law prevails if laws conflict.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- exclusive list: Only the federal government legislates on the exclusive list.
- residual list: Residual matters belong to the states.
- reserved list: That is not the usual name for shared powers.

questions.stem: A loose union of sovereign states that keep the right to withdraw is a
questions.explanation:
In a confederation members remain sovereign and may leave, as in Senegambia (1982–1989).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- federation: Members of a federation cannot secede at will.
- unitary state: A unitary state is a single state with a strong centre.
- protectorate: A protectorate is a territory under the protection of another state.

questions.stem: One merit of a unitary system of government is that it
questions.explanation:
With one centre of power, a unitary state can act quickly and apply the same laws everywhere.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gives regions equal power with the centre: That is a feature of federalism.
- allows member states to secede: That is a feature of a confederation.
- requires two levels of legislature: That is a federal feature and a cost, not a unitary merit.

options.label: A
options.content: gives regions equal power with the centre

options.label: C
options.content: promotes uniform laws and quick decisions

papers.title: Systems of Government: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on systems of government, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a parliamentary system, the head of government is the
questions.explanation:
Parliamentary systems have a dual executive: a ceremonial head of state and a prime minister who governs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- monarch: The monarch is a ceremonial head of state.
- speaker: The speaker presides over the legislature.
- chief justice: The chief justice heads the judiciary.

questions.stem: Collective responsibility is a feature of the
questions.explanation:
In a parliamentary system the cabinet stands or falls together and defends its decisions as one.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- presidential system: Presidential systems do not rely on cabinet collective responsibility to parliament.
- confederal system: Confederation is a form of state, not a system of executive responsibility.
- military system: Military regimes do not operate cabinet responsibility to a legislature.

questions.stem: According to Aristotle, the perverted form of rule by a few is
questions.explanation:
Aristotle contrasted aristocracy (the best few for all) with oligarchy (a few for themselves).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- aristocracy: Aristocracy is the good form of rule by a few.
- tyranny: Tyranny is the perverted form of rule by one.
- polity: Polity is the good form of rule by the many.

questions.stem: Government by religious leaders according to religious law is called
questions.explanation:
Theocracy is rule in the name of God or religious law.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- gerontocracy: Gerontocracy is rule by the elders.
- plutocracy: Plutocracy is rule by the wealthy.
- autocracy: Autocracy is rule by one person with unlimited power.

questions.stem: Sierra Leone became a republic on
questions.explanation:
On 19 April 1971 the British monarch ceased to be head of state.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 27 April 1961: That was independence.
- 1 October 1991: That was when the 1991 Constitution came into force.
- 29 April 1992: That was the NPRC coup.

papers.title: Democracy and Other Political Ideologies: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on democracy and other political ideologies, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: "Government of the people, by the people, for the people" is a definition of democracy given by
questions.explanation:
Abraham Lincoln used the phrase in his Gettysburg Address of 1863.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Karl Marx: Marx wrote about communism and class struggle.
- A. V. Dicey: Dicey wrote about the rule of law.
- Baron de Montesquieu: Montesquieu wrote about the separation of powers.

questions.stem: A direct vote by the electorate on a single public question is a
questions.explanation:
A referendum lets voters decide an issue directly, as in Sierra Leone's 1991 constitutional referendum.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- by-election: A by-election fills a vacant seat.
- primary election: A primary chooses a party's candidates.
- run-off: A run-off is a second round between leading candidates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a condition necessary for democracy to work well?
questions.explanation:
Free and fair elections need an impartial electoral body that all parties trust.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A ban on opposition parties: Banning opposition destroys democracy.
- Control of the press by the ruling party: A free press is needed for democracy.
- Life tenure for the president: Periodic elections are a feature of democracy.

options.label: B
options.content: Control of the press by the ruling party

questions.stem: The Communist Manifesto (1848) was written by
questions.explanation:
Marx and Engels set out the theory of class struggle and a classless communist society.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Adam Smith: Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations, a founding work of capitalism.
- Benito Mussolini: Mussolini founded fascism in Italy.
- John Locke: Locke was a liberal philosopher of the 1600s.

questions.stem: An economy in which both the state and private individuals own and run enterprises is a
questions.explanation:
Most modern states, including Sierra Leone, combine public and private enterprise.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- capitalist economy: Capitalism relies mainly on private ownership.
- communist economy: Communism aims at common ownership of all means of production.
- feudal economy: Feudalism was a medieval system of land held in return for service.

papers.title: The Executive: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the executive, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The civil service is often described as the
questions.explanation:
Civil servants stay in office when governments change, providing continuity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- political executive: The political executive is the President and ministers, who change with elections.
- nominal executive: A nominal executive is a ceremonial head of state.
- plural executive: A plural executive is a council that shares executive power.

questions.stem: The minimum age for a candidate for President under the 1991 Constitution of Sierra Leone is
questions.explanation:
A presidential candidate must be a citizen, at least 40 years old, and a member of a political party.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 21 years: 21 is the minimum age to be a Member of Parliament.
- 18 years: 18 is the voting age.
- 35 years: 35 is the age requirement in some other countries, such as the USA.

questions.stem: To win the presidential election in Sierra Leone in the first round, a candidate must obtain at least
questions.explanation:
If no candidate reaches 55%, a run-off is held between the top two.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50% of the valid votes cast: Sierra Leone sets a higher threshold of 55%.
- two-thirds of the valid votes cast: Two-thirds is the threshold for constitutional amendments in Parliament.
- the highest number of votes, whatever the share: That is simple majority; Sierra Leone requires 55% to avoid a run-off.

options.label: B
options.content: two-thirds of the valid votes cast

options.label: C
options.content: the highest number of votes, whatever the share

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the executive?
questions.explanation:
The executive carries out laws and policies and runs the administration.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Interpreting the constitution in disputes: That is a judicial function.
- Passing the Appropriation Act: Parliament passes the Appropriation Act.
- Hearing election petitions: Courts hear election petitions.

options.label: A
options.content: Implementing laws passed by the legislature

questions.stem: Executive power has grown in modern states mainly because of
questions.explanation:
Providing education, health and economic management needs a large, powerful executive.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the abolition of the civil service in most countries: The civil service has grown, not been abolished.
- the decline of political parties and party discipline: Party control actually strengthens executives.
- the reduction of government functions and spending: Government functions have expanded.

options.label: A
options.content: the abolition of the civil service in most countries

options.label: B
options.content: the expansion of welfare services and economic planning

options.label: C
options.content: the decline of political parties and party discipline

options.label: D
options.content: the reduction of government functions and spending

papers.title: The Legislature: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the legislature, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A legislature with two chambers is described as
questions.explanation:
Nigeria, the USA and Britain have bicameral legislatures.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- unicameral: Unicameral means one chamber.
- plural: Plural describes an executive council.
- federal: Federal describes a form of state, not the number of chambers.

questions.stem: At which stage of a bill are its general principles debated?
questions.explanation:
If the House rejects the principle at the second reading, the bill fails.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- First reading: At the first reading only the title is read.
- Committee stage: The committee examines the bill clause by clause.
- Report stage: The report stage considers the committee's amendments.

questions.stem: The officer who presides over the Parliament of Sierra Leone is the
questions.explanation:
The Speaker presides over sittings, keeps order and interprets the standing orders.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Clerk of Parliament: The Clerk is the chief administrative officer.
- Leader of Government Business: This leader manages government business but does not preside.
- Sergeant-at-Arms: The Sergeant-at-Arms keeps order and carries the Mace.

questions.stem: Paramount Chief Members of Parliament in Sierra Leone represent
questions.explanation:
There is one Paramount Chief Member of Parliament for each of the 14 provincial districts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- each of the 190 chiefdoms, one member for every chiefdom: There are only 14 PCMPs, not one per chiefdom.
- the Western Area Urban and Rural districts only: PCMPs come from the provincial districts.
- the political parties, in proportion to their votes: PCMPs are not party list members.

options.label: A
options.content: each of the 190 chiefdoms, one member for every chiefdom

options.label: B
options.content: the provincial districts, one member for each district

options.label: C
options.content: the Western Area Urban and Rural districts only

options.label: D
options.content: the political parties, in proportion to their votes

questions.stem: Parliament controls public spending after it has taken place mainly through the
questions.explanation:
The Public Accounts Committee examines the Auditor-General's report on how money was spent.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Committee of Selection: This committee chooses members of committees.
- Appointments Committee: This committee vets nominees for office.
- Committee of the Whole House: This is a sitting of all MPs, often on money bills, before spending.

papers.title: The Judiciary: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the judiciary, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The power of the courts to declare a law unconstitutional is called
questions.explanation:
Judicial review lets courts strike down laws and actions that conflict with the constitution.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- judicial precedent: Precedent means following earlier decisions.
- judicial immunity: Immunity protects judges from being sued for their decisions.
- appellate jurisdiction: That is the power to hear appeals.

questions.stem: Which of the following helps to ensure the independence of the judiciary?
questions.explanation:
Judges who cannot be removed at will can rule against the government without fear.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Appointment of judges by the ruling party: Party appointment undermines independence.
- Annual votes on judges' salaries by Parliament: Salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund to avoid this pressure.
- Membership of judges in political parties: Judges must stay out of party politics.

options.label: B
options.content: Appointment of judges by the ruling party

options.label: C
options.content: Annual votes on judges' salaries by Parliament

options.label: D
options.content: Membership of judges in political parties

questions.stem: The highest court in Sierra Leone is the
questions.explanation:
The Supreme Court, headed by the Chief Justice, is the final court of appeal and interprets the Constitution.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Court of Appeal: The Court of Appeal is below the Supreme Court.
- High Court: The High Court is below the Court of Appeal.
- Judicial Committee of the Privy Council: Appeals to the Privy Council ended in 1971.

options.label: D
options.content: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

questions.stem: Courts that apply customary law in the chiefdoms of Sierra Leone are
questions.explanation:
Local Courts deal with customary matters such as land, family and inheritance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Magistrate Courts: Magistrate Courts apply statute and common law in less serious cases.
- Courts martial: Courts martial try members of the armed forces.
- Commercial Courts: The Commercial Court handles business disputes in the High Court.

questions.stem: In Sierra Leone, judges of the superior courts are appointed by the President on the advice of the
questions.explanation:
The JLSC advises and Parliament approves, so no single person chooses the judges.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Public Service Commission, without any parliamentary approval: The Public Service Commission deals with public officers, not judges.
- Electoral Commission, after consulting the political parties: The Electoral Commission conducts elections.
- Political Parties Regulation Commission, with the Speaker's consent: The PPRC regulates political parties.

options.label: A
options.content: Public Service Commission, without any parliamentary approval

options.label: B
options.content: Electoral Commission, after consulting the political parties

options.label: C
options.content: Political Parties Regulation Commission, with the Speaker's consent

options.label: D
options.content: Judicial and Legal Service Commission, subject to Parliament's approval
